What Katteb can help you write

In this guide, the focus is a practical writing process: gather evidence, prepare a brief, review a draft, and publish useful original content.

The tool may be worth evaluating when a blank page slows you down, when your ideas are scattered across notes, or when a first draft needs a clearer structure. It is less helpful if you expect it to invent experience you do not have. For a service page, your real process, delivery terms, examples, and customer questions remain essential inputs. Software cannot supply those business facts accurately without you.

Start with the reader's actual task

Describe who the article is for and what they should be able to do after reading. A guide for a new online shop owner needs different examples from a guide for an experienced agency editor. Write the task plainly: compare two options, set up a process, avoid a common mistake, or decide whether a tool fits a budget. This makes the brief more useful than a topic alone.

For example, a freelancer writing about preparing a content brief could focus on a small business owner commissioning their first article. That reader needs an explanation of audience, purpose, source material, tone, and approval steps. They probably do not need a long history of content marketing. When you define the task first, you can reject sections that add length without helping the reader make progress.

Build a source brief before drafting

Collect the information the article genuinely depends on. For a software comparison, start with official documentation and current product pages. For your own service, use your approved process and delivery details. Add a note beside each source explaining what it supports. A link alone is not enough: a pricing page may support a plan description but cannot support a claim that every user saves a particular number of hours.

Separate stable guidance from details that can change. Your explanation of writing a useful introduction may stay relevant for a long time. A price, product limit, or integration needs a date and a fresh check. If you cannot verify a detail, leave it out or explain the uncertainty. It is better to publish a narrower accurate guide than a broad article full of confident assumptions.

Keep evidence close to the claim

When a paragraph relies on a source, keep a note beside it during editing. Ask whether the source directly supports the wording and whether any conditions have been omitted. A page describing one paid plan does not establish that a feature is included in every plan. This habit is useful even when an AI tool supplies references, because a real link can still be attached to an unsupported sentence.

Write a brief that produces a usable first draft

Include the audience, main question, intended outcome, language, tone, approximate length, and important source facts. Add what the draft must avoid, such as invented testimonials, unsupported performance claims, or outdated prices. Give the tool a simple outline if you already understand the topic. That is usually a better starting point than asking for a comprehensive article and hoping the right priorities appear automatically.

An illustrative instruction could ask for a plain English guide for a freelance designer choosing a project handover process. Supply the actual handover steps, explain that the reader is a beginner, and request examples using ordinary client work. Ask for short paragraphs and direct answers to likely questions. Keep private client names and confidential project material out of a shared environment unless the access arrangement has been verified as appropriate.

Review the outline before expanding it

Look at the headings as a complete journey. Does the reader receive the basic answer early? Are the steps in an order they can follow? Does each section answer a distinct question? Remove repeated introductions and headings that say the same thing in slightly different words. A shorter outline with clear purpose usually gives you a stronger article than a long outline built around every possible keyword variation.

Search results can help you notice missing questions, but competing pages are not a script to copy. Look for recurring subjects and ask whether your reader needs them. Then add your own examples, experience, and explanation. For a separate content planning workflow, you can review our Frase group buy guide. The aim is useful coverage, not matching a competitor paragraph for paragraph.

Fact-check a draft one claim at a time

Make a pass through the draft looking only for factual statements. Highlight names, dates, numbers, product features, comparisons, and promises about results. Check them against the source brief. If an important statement has no support, investigate it or remove it. Do not let smooth language make a weak claim feel more reliable than it is. An editor's job includes noticing what the draft cannot actually establish.

Katteb presents fact-checking tools, but a fact-checked label should not replace your own review. Inspect references, read the relevant passage, and check whether the context matches the sentence. An old source may have been correct when published and still be unsuitable for a current plan comparison. For work with serious consequences, use the appropriate qualified reviewer rather than treating a writing assistant as the final authority.

Add the experience that makes the article yours

Replace general advice with examples you can explain. If you have handled a difficult project handover, describe the useful lesson without exposing a client. If you tested a workflow, say what you tested and what you observed. Avoid implying that you used a product when you only reviewed its documentation. Readers benefit from a clear distinction between an observed result, an illustrative example, and a suggestion for their own testing.

A useful article often includes small details that a generic draft misses: what to prepare before starting, where a beginner is likely to get stuck, and how to recognize a finished result. Add those details during editing. They do not need dramatic claims or impressive statistics. A clear explanation of one practical problem can be more valuable than several paragraphs promising effortless success.

Edit for natural language and brand voice

Read a section aloud and notice where you would never speak that way to a customer. Replace formal filler with ordinary words. Break a sentence if it contains several unrelated ideas. Keep specialist terms when they help, but explain them the first time. A friendly brand voice is not created by adding enthusiastic adjectives to every paragraph; it comes from useful examples, clear decisions, and consistent language.

Give the draft a small set of voice rules. You might ask for direct language, short introductions, specific examples, and no invented quotes. Then review the result yourself. If your audience is multilingual, have a fluent reader check tone and meaning in the final language. Translation and language settings can help produce a draft, but they do not establish that a phrase sounds natural in every market.

Use keywords where they answer real questions

Choose one main search intent and a small set of supporting topics. Place the main phrase naturally in the title, introduction, and a relevant heading when it fits. Use related terms in the sections where they add meaning. If a question is about the Katteb lifetime deal, answer the difference between shared duration and a lifetime purchase directly. Repeating the phrase throughout unrelated paragraphs would make the guide less useful.

After drafting, check that each important search question has a clear answer. Do not chase a particular keyword density or treat an optimization score as proof of ranking.
